Situations that put my body under stress

Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I have permanently changed for the worse

issues.item: Triggers: Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
issues.explanation: The trigger 'When people say things like my ex' is difficult to reconcile with a military trauma profile and the rest of the selected items, which center on combat/injury/hypervigilance cues. It introduces an interpersonal/romantic reminder theme that is otherwise unsupported by the memory, threat, appraisal, and strategy items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: 'I feel permanently humiliated by what happened' is not impossible after military trauma, but in this profile it sits somewhat apart from the rest of the formulation, which is dominated by injury cues, hypervigilance, fragmentation, outsider beliefs, and self-blame. The combination is not a direct contradiction on its own, but paired with the relationship-reminder trigger it suggests a mismatched interpersonal/shame theme that is insufficiently anchored elsewhere in the profile.

vignette: Lukas, a 28-year-old social-media manager from a small Bavarian town, returned home after a three-month tour in Afghanistan. On the flight home he watched the silhouettes of soldiers, many bearing fresh wounds, glide past the window. The sight of visible injuries, the constant hum of a helicopter engine over the runway, and the collective shudder when a drone buzzed overhead all struck him with a sudden, almost physical shock. Each flash of a wounded comrade's face or every distant thud of rotor blades became a trigger that pulled him back to the front line. When a colleague asked him to join a client video call, he hesitated and walked away, citing fatigue. The discomfort of wearing a crisp office blazer that resembled a uniform seemed to him a thin line between civilian life and the battlefield. These triggers set off a chain that sent Lukas spiraling into a heightened state of vigilance: he could not sleep, his heart would pound at the slightest rustle, and even a light touch from a partner's hand sent him to the edge of panic. The memory of the battlefield, fragmented and devoid of a clear image, lodged itself behind each trigger, leaving him convinced that he was permanently an outsider, that no one could have endured what he had. The memory that swirled within him was not a single vivid recollection but a patchwork of disjointed fragments-screams, gunfire, the metallic tang of blood-each fragment a sudden jolt that felt like a flash in the dark. The absence of a coherent image only amplified his sense of threat. He would find himself staring at the white line of a road while driving with colleagues, the line suddenly appearing as the boundary between safety and danger. The intrusive recollection would trigger a startle response to touch, forcing him to rehearse every sentence he might utter before any conversation, as if a single misstep could unravel the fragile peace he managed to hold. The fragmented memory also fed his negative appraisals: he felt he had been permanently damaged, that the world had turned against him, and that no other soldier had ever endured such horrors. When Lukas tried to engage with his job, the threat of being confronted by everyday stimuli-driving, sudden noises, the hum of equipment-made him constantly on guard. The awareness that any sudden movement or unfamiliar sound could recall a battlefield episode led him to avoid physically stressful situations, such as the high-energy client pitches that demanded a full body presence. He began rehearsing his dialogue, scripting each answer so that no question would surprise him, a method that both shielded him and kept him emotionally distant. Every time the threat intensified, he would retreat further into his rehearsed scripts, and each retreat heightened his sense of threat again. Even a quiet morning coffee with his partner felt like a potential trigger; his partner's casual touch would ignite a startle that made him retreat into his rehearsed script of excuses, further solidifying the cycle of avoidance. His maladaptive strategies seeped into every corner of his life. By avoiding situations that reminded him of the war-such as wearing a blazer or handling a physical object-he inadvertently increased his sense of isolation, reinforcing the belief that he was permanently different. Each rehearsal of conversation became a rehearsal of his perceived inadequacy, a way to convince himself that he was still an outsider. When he avoided driving with colleagues, he became even more anxious at the thought of a potential trigger on the road, and the anxiety fed back into the memory fragments that now surfaced in even the most ordinary moments. The more he clung to these strategies, the more they intensified his threat vigilance, and the greater the risk that he would interpret ordinary stimuli as dangerous. Lukas's present request for help came after a recent incident where he collapsed during a client presentation, overwhelmed by the sudden roar of a laptop fan and a colleague's laugh. He realized that his avoidance had cost him a promotion and strained his relationship. He fears that if he does not break this cycle, he will lose the life he has built-his job, his partner, his sense of belonging. He hopes therapy can help him unlearn the rehearsed scripts, quiet the perpetual alertness, and see that the battlefield's echoes no longer dictate his reality.
